planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Allred is a dual-purpose plum grown for both its dramatic red-purple foliage and its sweet-tart, red-skinned fruit, and benefits from a second compatible plum nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible plum cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set. Allred is a hybrid plum valued as much for its landscape impact as its harvest, holding rich red-purple foliage color through the growing season that rivals purpleleaf ornamental plums, while still producing sweet-tart, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit good for fresh eating and preserves. Its dual-purpose nature makes it a good choice for a home orchard that also wants ornamental structure in the landscape. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that improves airflow and fruit quality.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Plum Variety Selection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Plum Variety Recommendations
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Plum Culture for the Gulf South

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Utah Sweet is grown for arils that are notably sweeter and less tart than Wonderful, with softer, more tender seeds.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; pomegranate is highly drought-tolerant once established and performs well on minimal irrigation in well-drained Gulf South soils. Utah Sweet is valued for pink-tinged skin and pulp with a notably sweeter, less tart flavor than the widely grown Wonderful pomegranate, along with softer, more tender seeds that make the arils easier to eat fresh without the firmer crunch typical of many other pomegranate cultivars. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will fruit, though yields can improve with cross-pollination from a second cultivar. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then ease back as fruit nears ripeness to help prevent splitting, and harvest when the fruit gives a dull, metallic sound when tapped.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pomegranate Fact Sheet
University of California Cooperative Extension — Pomegranate Cultivars
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranate Production

common_name: Hardy Chicago Fig (Widely Grown Cold-Hardy Home-Garden Fig)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or rooted-cutting trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hardy Chicago is one of the most widely grown home-garden fig cultivars in the country, valued for reliable production and root hardiness that lets it resprout after a hard freeze even where the top growth is killed back.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and mulch well over the root zone. Hardy Chicago is one of the most widely planted fig cultivars for home gardens across the country, prized for dependable, heavy production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, strawberry-red pulp, along with unusual root hardiness that allows it to resprout from the base and still produce a crop even after a winter cold enough to kill the top growth to the ground. This resilience has made it a favorite starter fig for gardeners in climates on the edge of reliable fig hardiness, though in the milder winters of the Gulf South it typically grows as a full, unpruned multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Harvest figs when they soften, droop on the stem, and develop full color, picking every day or two during the height of the season since ripe figs do not store well.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fact Sheet
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Fig Culture for the Gulf South
North Carolina State Extension — Fig Cultivars

common_name: Ichi Ki Kei Jiro Persimmon (Self-Fertile Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Ichi Ki Kei Jiro is a self-fertile, non-astringent Asian persimmon that can be eaten crisp like an apple as soon as it colors, without needing to soften first.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and stake young trees until well established. Ichi Ki Kei Jiro is a compact, heavy-bearing Japanese persimmon cultivar belonging to the non-astringent group, meaning the fruit can be harvested and eaten crisp and sweet as soon as it reaches full orange color, unlike astringent Asian and American persimmons that must fully soften before they are palatable. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will produce a full crop without a pollinator, and its naturally smaller stature suits home orchards with limited space. Thin fruit if the tree sets an especially heavy crop to improve size, and harvest by clipping fruit from the branch rather than pulling, since the stem can tear the skin.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Persimmon Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Persimmon Culture

common_name: Rosseyanka Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Non-Astringent American-Asian Hybrid Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Rosseyanka is a cold-hardy hybrid of American and Asian persimmon developed in Ukraine, combining strong hardiness with fruit that becomes non-astringent when firm-ripe.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, staking young trees until established. Rosseyanka is a hybrid between the native American persimmon and Asian persimmon, developed in Ukraine to combine the cold hardiness of the American species with fruit quality closer to Asian persimmons, notably becoming non-astringent and pleasant to eat while still firm rather than requiring the full softening American persimmons need. It is a productive, vigorous tree well suited to a wider hardiness range than most pure Asian persimmon cultivars while still offering good fruit size and flavor. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop, and harvest by clipping the fruit from the branch to avoid tearing the skin at the stem.
sources: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — American Persimmon
California Rare Fruit Growers — Persimmon Fact Sheet
